name: Config Service
tagline: A typed, versioned configuration store that replaced a shared YAML file and its merge conflicts.

seo.title: Config Service — Martin Zachariassen
seo.description: A typed, versioned configuration store built in Go and PostgreSQL, replacing a shared YAML file across services.

cover.alt: A config publish view showing a timeout and retry value changed and validated against a schema before publishing.
cover.caption: A config change is validated and published, not merged and deployed.

outcome.label: Incidents from a bad value, since

summary: A dozen services shared one YAML file in a config repo, edited by hand and deployed by CI. Merge conflicts and silent typos were routine. I built a small typed config service with schema validation and an audit log, so a bad value fails at publish time instead of at runtime in a service nobody was watching.

blocks.value: Twelve services read their settings from a single file in a repository they all deployed from. Changing one timeout meant a pull request against a file four other teams were editing that week, a review from whoever was free rather than whoever knew, and a deploy that carried everyone else's pending changes out with yours.

blocks.title: How it actually went wrong
items: Conflicts in a format with no structure to merge along — YAML is indentation, and a badly resolved conflict is usually still valid YAML.
The same timeout: 30 meaning seconds in one service and milliseconds in the next, with nothing anywhere to say which.
A misspelled key. The service read its default instead, started cleanly, and behaved strangely for two days.
No way to answer "when did this change, and who decided that?" without reading a repository's history and guessing.

sections.label: Approach
sections.heading: Let the service own the schema, and validate at publish

blocks.value: Each service declares the configuration it reads and owns that declaration. Publishing a value validates it against the declaration and stores it as a new version — the store is append-only, so the value it replaced is always still there to go back to. Services subscribe and see a change within a couple of seconds, which is the part that matters: a config change stopped being a deploy.

blocks.caption: A key with no declaration cannot be published, and a declared key cannot be published with the wrong type or outside its bounds. Both of those used to be things you found out about in production.
lines: // Declared once, by the service that reads it: type, bounds,
// and a default that is known to be safe.
// Reads are typed and cannot fail here: a value that would not
// satisfy the declaration was refused at publish time, so there
// is no error to handle at the call site and no default to

blocks.title: The part I got wrong twice
blocks.value: Delivering a change to subscribers was harder than storing one, and I underestimated it in both directions. The first version polled every thirty seconds, which was fine until a service running two hundred pods made it the busiest query in the database. The second used the database's own notifications and quietly lost updates whenever a connection dropped. What runs today polls one version counter and only fetches when it moves — less elegant than either, and the first one that has never woken anybody.

sections.label: Result
sections.heading: Config errors caught before rollout, not after

blocks.value: Every config change is validated against the owning service's schema before it publishes, and every publish is attributed and reversible. The class of incident caused by a bad config value reaching production dropped to zero in the following year.

The change I did not anticipate was to how people behaved. When changing a value took nine minutes and a deploy, values were changed rarely and in batches, which is exactly the shape of change that is hardest to attribute when something breaks. At four seconds and a one-click revert, they get changed one at a time — and one at a time is the version you can reason about.
